Proof by Cases and Existence Proofs

Split the plane into four regions and handle one case at a time. Then meet a proof that shows existence without revealing which side holds.

A case split must leave no gap. Each region's computation is easy. Miss one region and the whole proof collapses. Existence proofs are different: 'it exists' can be shown without producing it.

For example, a 🧑 friend may stand east or west of your house. Either way, the distance home ignores the sign. Checking both directions is exactly a proof by cases.

Examples & Exercises

Prove completely by cases: ∣xy∣=∣x∣ ∣y∣|xy| = |x|\,|y|∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣ for all real x,yx, yx,y.

Cover all four sign cases (the zero case folds into case 1) and apply the definition of ∣t∣|t|∣t∣ (ttt if t≥0t \ge 0t≥0, −t-t−t if t<0t < 0t<0) directly in each case.

∣xy∣=∣x∣ ∣y∣∀x,y∈R|xy| = |x|\,|y| \qquad \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣∀x,y∈R
x<0<y  ⇒  ∣xy∣=−(xy)=(−x)⋅y=∣x∣ ∣y∣x < 0 < y \;\Rightarrow\; |xy| = -(xy) = (-x) \cdot y = |x|\,|y|x<0<y⇒∣xy∣=−(xy)=(−x)⋅y=∣x∣∣y∣
Show proof

  1. Case 1: x≥0x \ge 0x≥0, y≥0y \ge 0y≥0.

    Then xy≥0xy \ge 0xy≥0, so ∣xy∣=xy|xy| = xy∣xy∣=xy.

    Also ∣x∣=x|x| = x∣x∣=x and ∣y∣=y|y| = y∣y∣=y, so ∣x∣ ∣y∣=xy|x|\,|y| = xy∣x∣∣y∣=xy — both sides agree.

    (The case x=0x = 0x=0 or y=0y = 0y=0 folds in here: xy=0xy = 0xy=0 gives ∣xy∣=0=∣x∣ ∣y∣|xy| = 0 = |x|\,|y|∣xy∣=0=∣x∣∣y∣.)

  2. Case 2: x>0x > 0x>0, y<0y < 0y<0.

    Then xy<0xy < 0xy<0, so ∣xy∣=−(xy)|xy| = -(xy)∣xy∣=−(xy).

    Since −xy=x⋅(−y)-xy = x \cdot (-y)−xy=x⋅(−y) and ∣x∣=x|x| = x∣x∣=x, ∣y∣=−y|y| = -y∣y∣=−y, we get ∣x∣ ∣y∣=x⋅(−y)|x|\,|y| = x \cdot (-y)∣x∣∣y∣=x⋅(−y) — both sides agree.

  3. Case 3: x<0x < 0x<0, y>0y > 0y>0.

    Then xy<0xy < 0xy<0, so ∣xy∣=−(xy)=(−x)⋅y|xy| = -(xy) = (-x) \cdot y∣xy∣=−(xy)=(−x)⋅y.

    Since ∣x∣=−x|x| = -x∣x∣=−x and ∣y∣=y|y| = y∣y∣=y, we get ∣x∣ ∣y∣=(−x)⋅y|x|\,|y| = (-x) \cdot y∣x∣∣y∣=(−x)⋅y — both sides agree.

  4. Case 4: x<0x < 0x<0, y<0y < 0y<0.

    Then xy>0xy > 0xy>0, so ∣xy∣=xy|xy| = xy∣xy∣=xy.

    Since ∣x∣=−x|x| = -x∣x∣=−x and ∣y∣=−y|y| = -y∣y∣=−y, we get ∣x∣ ∣y∣=(−x)⋅(−y)=xy|x|\,|y| = (-x) \cdot (-y) = xy∣x∣∣y∣=(−x)⋅(−y)=xy — both sides agree.

    The four cases cover every (x,y)∈R2(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2(x,y)∈R2 with nothing left out, so ∣xy∣=∣x∣ ∣y∣|xy| = |x|\,|y|∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣ holds for all real x,yx, yx,y. ∎

Prove non-constructively: there exist irrational numbers a,ba, ba,b with aba^bab rational.

Put c=22c = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}c=2​2​ and split into "if ccc is rational / if ccc is irrational".

Rigorously justify the exponent step (22)2=22⋅2=22=2\big(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\big)^{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2(2​2​)2​=2​2​⋅2​=2​2=2 from the power law (uv)w=uvw(u^v)^w = u^{vw}(uv)w=uvw (u>0u > 0u>0), and explain why this proof is non-constructive.

c=22≈1.6325269194381528c = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.6325269194381528c=2​2​≈1.6325269194381528
c∈Q⇒a=b=2;c∉Q⇒a=c, b=2, ab=2c \in \mathbb{Q} \Rightarrow a = b = \sqrt{2}; \qquad c \notin \mathbb{Q} \Rightarrow a = c,\ b = \sqrt{2},\ a^b = 2c∈Q⇒a=b=2​;c∈/Q⇒a=c, b=2​, ab=2
Show proof

  1. That 2\sqrt{2}2​ is irrational is known (see the 'sqrt2-irrational' scene problems).

    Put c=22c = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}c=2​2​ — an irrational power of an irrational.

    Without asking whether ccc is rational or irrational, split into two cases.

  2. Case 1: ccc is rational. Put a=b=2a = b = \sqrt{2}a=b=2​: then a,ba, ba,b are irrational and ab=22=ca^b = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} = cab=2​2​=c is rational — done.

  3. Case 2: ccc is irrational.

    Put a=ca = ca=c, b=2b = \sqrt{2}b=2​: then a,ba, ba,b are irrational, and applying the power law (uv)w=uvw(u^v)^w = u^{vw}(uv)w=uvw (valid for real u>0u > 0u>0 and real v,wv, wv,w) with u=2u = \sqrt{2}u=2​, v=w=2v = w = \sqrt{2}v=w=2​ gives ab=(22)2=22⋅2=22=2a^b = \big(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\big)^{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}^{2} = 2ab=(2​2​)2​=2​2​⋅2​=2​2=2 — rational.

    Numerically too: c2≈2.0000000000c^{\sqrt{2}} \approx 2.0000000000c2​≈2.0000000000.

  4. In either case irrational a,ba, ba,b exist with aba^bab rational, completing the proof.

    The proof is non-constructive: it never says which pair (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) works — (2,2)(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2})(2​,2​) if case 1 holds, (c,2)(c, \sqrt{2})(c,2​) if case 2 holds — because whether ccc is rational or irrational is never decided anywhere in the proof.

    (The Gelfond–Schneider theorem does imply ccc is in fact transcendental, hence irrational, so case 2 is the true one — but the proof above never uses that.) ∎

Prove by cases (nnn even / nnn odd): every integer square is congruent to 000 or 111 modulo 444.

Use this to show that x2+y2=3x^2 + y^2 = 3x2+y2=3 has no integer solutions.

n=2k⇒n2=4k2≡0(mod4);n=2k+1⇒n2=4(k2+k)+1≡1(mod4)n = 2k \Rightarrow n^2 = 4k^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4; \qquad n = 2k+1 \Rightarrow n^2 = 4(k^2+k)+1 \equiv 1 \pmod 4n=2k⇒n2=4k2≡0(mod4);n=2k+1⇒n2=4(k2+k)+1≡1(mod4)
x2+y2(mod4)∈{0,1,2}∌3x^2 + y^2 \pmod 4 \in \{0, 1, 2\} \not\ni 3x2+y2(mod4)∈{0,1,2}∋3
Show proof

  1. Case 1: nnn is even, n=2kn = 2kn=2k (k∈Zk \in \mathbb{Z}k∈Z). Then n2=4k2n^2 = 4k^2n2=4k2, so n2≡0(mod4)n^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4n2≡0(mod4).

  2. Case 2: nnn is odd, n=2k+1n = 2k+1n=2k+1.

    Then n2=4k2+4k+1=4(k2+k)+1n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 4(k^2 + k) + 1n2=4k2+4k+1=4(k2+k)+1, so n2≡1(mod4)n^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4n2≡1(mod4).

    The two cases cover every integer with nothing left out, so every integer square is 000 or 111 modulo 444.

  3. Now suppose x2+y2=3x^2 + y^2 = 3x2+y2=3 had an integer solution (proof by contradiction).

    Since x2(mod4),y2(mod4)∈{0,1}x^2 \pmod 4, y^2 \pmod 4 \in \{0, 1\}x2(mod4),y2(mod4)∈{0,1}, their sum x2+y2(mod4)x^2 + y^2 \pmod 4x2+y2(mod4) lies in {0,1,2}\{0, 1, 2\}{0,1,2}: 0+0=00+0 = 00+0=0, 0+1=10+1 = 10+1=1, 1+1=21+1 = 21+1=2.

    But 3≡3(mod4)3 \equiv 3 \pmod 43≡3(mod4) is not in this set — a contradiction.

    Hence x2+y2=3x^2 + y^2 = 3x2+y2=3 has no integer solutions. ∎
